Sista Paramitaa | Nunik Dwi Kusumawatia | Achmad Kautsarb | Eunike Febrianti Sanjayaa aDepartment of Management, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Indonesia. bDigital Business Program, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Indonesia. Abstract This paper examines the impact of presidential elections on stock return volatility in four selected Sub-South East Asian stock markets: Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines. Using a generalised autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity (GARCH) model, this study incorporates pre- and post-election dummy variables to assess the effect of presidential elections on market volatility. The findings reveal that heightened uncertainty before the elections significantly increases stock market volatility across all four countries. Additionally, the study highlights that investors' limited understanding of post-election government policies further drives market volatility for up to 90 days after the election. In contrast to previous research focused on individual leading countries, this paper offers a comparative analysis of countries with similar political and economic conditions, providing new insights into the broader regional effects of elections on stock market behaviour. Keywords: volatility, presidential elections, sub-south east asia, stock markets, politic uncertainty 1. Introduction Over the years, extensive research has been dedicated to identifying the variables contributing to the dynamics of stock market volatility, encompassing macroeconomic, microeconomic, and behavioural aspects. Macroeconomic fundamentals significantly influence both short-term and long-term stock market volatility. For instance, Engle et al. (2013) Emphasise the importance of inflation and industrial output growth in understanding the dynamics of this volatility. Similarly, Pindyck (2004) highlights the significance of volatility in commodity markets and its relationship to market dynamics and economic conditions. Macroeconomic shocks, such as shifts in monetary policy or global economic conditions, also influence market behaviour, as explored by Bekaert et al. (2013), who examine the effects of global risk factors and macroeconomic news on stock returns. Schwert (1989) provides a long-term perspective on how historical economic events and recessions contribute to stock market volatility. In microeconomics, research often examines the relationship between stock market volatility, financial metrics, and intrinsic asset value. Tarlie (2013) explores how discount rates and returns on capital—key determinants of a firm’s intrinsic value—affect stock price dynamics and volatility. In addition, models explaining speculative return volatility have been proposed, with Zhu (2007) emphasising the role of persistent and volatile components in determining stock return prices. Behavioural finance has also made substantial contributions to understanding stock market volatility. Fushing et al. (2012) examine how collective investor behaviour, particularly during periods of high-volume trading, can drive significant volatility in the stock market. Their findings suggest that market dynamics are strongly influenced by large groups of participants whose trading behaviour drives volatility. Similarly, Dimpfl & Jank (2016) show a strong correlation between retail investor attention, as reflected in internet search queries, and market volatility, underscoring the important role of behavioural factors. Despite this extensive body of research, one area that has received less attention is the impact of political events, such as presidential elections, on stock return volatility. Political factors, particularly presidential elections, are significant drivers of volatility dynamics in financial markets (Mei & Guo, 2004). Elections often introduce uncertainty into the market as investors react to potential changes in government policy, the economic outlook, and the regulatory environment (Goodell et al., 2020). Presidential elections engender market anxiety as investors form and revise their expectations regarding future macroeconomic policy, leading to increased implied stock market volatility (Goodell & Vähämaa, 2013). Elections have been shown to be reflected in pre-election common stock returns, with stock market volatility and average returns rising when the election does not have a candidate with a dominant lead (Li & Born, 2006). During election periods, markets may experience heightened volatility as outcomes become uncertain and investor sentiment shifts based on the perceived impact of different Multidiscip. Sci. J. Election outcomes, including election surprises, have been found to increase volatility but have no significant effect on excess returns, with the winning party's orientation not affecting excess returns or volatility significantly (Arin et al., 2022). In ASEAN, the rise of electoral democracy began around the early 1930s and gained further momentum by the 1960s. However, democracy in the region does not strictly follow the Western liberal model. While some ASEAN countries incorporate elements such as elections, parliaments, and political parties, these features are often adapted to align with local traditions, political cultures, and power dynamics. Western-style democracy is most evident in Indonesia, with its open proportional electoral system (Nugroho et al., 2024), and the Philippines, which employs a party-list system along with guest candidacy to foster electoral competitiveness (Lee & Chung, 2004). Malaysia, although incorporating democratic processes, utilises a district-based electoral system that deviates from Western proportional representation models (Nugroho et al., 2024). Hybrid or localised forms of democracy are seen in Thailand and Singapore. Thailand has restructured its electoral system to promote competitiveness while restricting non-partisan candidates to preserve party stability (Lee & Chung, 2004). Singapore, influenced by non-Western values such as Confucianism and centralised governance, maintains a tightly controlled electoral environment (Rodan, 2012). Both Malaysia and Singapore exemplify hybrid regimes, where democratic institutions coexist with authoritarian practices, allowing limited political competition under dominant ruling parties (Weiss, 2014). Other ASEAN countries, Vietnam, Laos, Brunei, Myanmar, and Cambodia, continue to operate under non-democratic systems, with restricted political pluralism and centralised authority. Focusing on economic significance within ASEAN, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Thailand stand out as the three largest economies in the region, making them vital for economic studies (Napathorn & Kuruvilla, 2017). The Philippines also boasts a robust economy and is part of the original ASEAN-5, known for strong economic growth (Manasan, 2019). These Countries also have their political stability (Freedman, 2011; Hadiz, 2007) and the presence of clientelistic practices (Aspinall & Hicken, 2020; Tomsa & Ufen, 2012). The most recent information from the World Bank Data (2023) indicates that Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows as a percentage of GDP are 4.5% for the Bursa Malaysia stock exchange and 3.5% for the Indonesia Stock Exchange. The Philippine Stock Exchange follows closely with 2.5% and the Stock Exchange of Thailand with 2.2%. Nonetheless, the complexities of electoral processes in these nations further complicate the relationship between elections and market behaviour. In Indonesia, election outcomes often lead to disputes, which can increase stock crash risks (Kusdarini et al., 2022; Wijaya & Adawiyah, 2019). In Malaysia, elections increase stock volatility, particularly in the pre-election period, and affect market efficiency (Jiun, 2018; Liew & Rowland, 2016). By 2023, Thailand's election, marked by political issues, caused a significant stock market decline, with political uncertainty also increasing volatility (Bowes, 2018; Khositkulporn et al., 2017; Prukumpai et al., 2022). Similarly, the Philippines faced market volatility due to political instability during elections (Macrohon et al., 2022). The aim of this paper is to examine the effect of presidential elections on stock return volatility in a cross-section of sub- ASEAN countries. This study employs several ways to analyse the presidential elections on stock volatility. Following Musah et al. (2023), first, we run pre-whitening data; second, we filter the data to make sure all the data is free from outliers and missing data, and then we use the LogL information criterion. Finally, we run the GARCH model. GARCH models to measure the impact of political events, including presidential elections, on stock return volatility (Carnahan & Saiegh, 2021; Jiun, 2018; Koulakiotis et al., 2016; Musah et al., 2023). To see any leverage effect, we analyse the EGARCH and the dummy variable using GJR-GARCH to see the reaction 90 pre-election and post-election. This study has several contributions. First, it contributes to the literature by providing comparative evidence on how presidential election uncertainty affects stock return volatility in the sub-ASEAN market. The significance of this paper is highlighted in the following ways. Firstly, unlike previous studies in the sub-region that are country and election-specific, the present study provides a broader picture of the impact of presidential elections on stock return volatility in the sub-ASEAN sub- region. The study provides evidence of commonalities and differences in the impact of presidential elections on sub-ASEAN stock markets. Secondly, the comparative evidence provided by this paper provides risk-averse investors with a better understanding of the risks associated with investing in various sub-ASEAN stock markets during periods of presidential elections and the opportunity for portfolio diversification. 2. Materials and Methods In this study, a robust three-step methodological approach is employed. First, in line with the methodology of Gulen & Mayhew (2000), we address the issue of potential autocorrelation in the return series, which is often associated with thin trading. A first-order autoregressive model is applied to mitigate this, and the residuals are extracted to form a filtered series. Second, we utilise multiple criteria to determine the most suitable generalised autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity (GARCH)-type model for each country. GARCH-type models are preferred for their ability to capture key features of financial time series, including volatility clustering, leverage effects, and long memory, which linear models typically fail to explain. Third, the selected GARCH-type model is then employed to estimate the second moment of the return distribution. This estimation process includes pre- and post-presidential election dummy variables, allowing for the analysis of the impact of presidential https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Akbar et al. The GARCH model is effective for capturing general volatility clustering in financial time series data (Khan, 2024; Guo et al., 2022), but often fails to account for asymmetries in the data, particularly during periods of high volatility (Sun and Yu, 2020). This limitation is because GARCH assumes a symmetric response of volatility to positive and negative shocks, which is not always realistic in financial markets where negative shocks (e.g., bad news) tend to increase volatility more than positive shocks. EGARCH (Exponential GARCH) model is designed to capture both asymmetry and leverage, accommodating the negative correlation between return shocks and subsequent shocks to volatility (McAleer and Hafner, 2014). Models address this by incorporating mechanisms that allow for asymmetric effects, thus better capturing the "leverage effect" (McAleer and Hafner, 2014) where negative returns increase future volatility more than positive returns. The GJR-GARCH (Glosten- Jagannathan-Runkle GARCH) model generalises asymmetric GARCH models, introducing multiple thresholds and making the asymmetric effect time-dependent, thus providing flexibility in capturing asymmetric effects (McAleer and Hafner, 2014). Studies have shown that these asymmetric models provide better forecasting performance for volatile markets, especially when fat-tailed and skewed distributions are present (Liu and Hung, 2010). Descriptive statistics and unit root results of filtered series The table 3 offers descriptive statistics and unit root test results for market return series from Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines. The mean and median values of market return across Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines indicate relatively small average returns, which is typical for financial time series data. The standard deviation values suggest that Thailand experienced the highest market volatility while Malaysia had the lowest. This finding shows that emerging markets often exhibit higher volatility than more developed markets. The negative skewness values across all markets suggest that the returns are skewed to the left, indicating a higher probability of extreme negative returns. This is consistent with the stylised facts of financial returns, which tend to be non-normally distributed with fat tails and asymmetry. The high kurtosis values, especially in Thailand, reinforce the presence of extreme returns, a common feature in emerging markets due to factors like economic shocks or political instability such as lack of freedom of expression and forced selection of candidates by one party, as highlighted by Harvey (1995) and it affects the investors concernedly. The significant results of the Jarque-Bera test across all markets imply that the return distributions deviate from normality. This finding supports that financial time series often exhibit leptokurtosis and skewness, deviating from the normal distribution assumption commonly used in financial models. The rejection of normality is a well-documented phenomenon in the literature, as seen in works by Cont (2001), who discusses the prevalence of non-Gaussian distributions in asset returns. This research is included in the non-Gaussian category because the data obtained is non-normal, so using this method will make it easier to obtain more suitable data for research. The ARCH LM test results indicate significant autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH) effects in all four markets. This suggests that past volatility can be used to predict future volatility, a characteristic often observed in financial time series. The presence of ARCH effects is consistent with findings from (Engle, 1982), who first introduced the concept and demonstrated its applicability in modelling financial market volatility. Similarly, the GARCH effect, denoted by β, is also significant for all the markets, indicating high volatility persistence. The β values are close to or exceed 0.8 for all markets, suggesting that they tend to remain elevated for a considerable period once volatility spikes. This persistence is particularly evident in the Malaysian market, where the β value is the highest, implying that volatility is more enduring than in other markets. The leverage effect, represented by Γ, is significant across all markets, indicating that negative shocks (such as bad news) have a greater impact on increasing volatility than positive shocks. This asymmetric response to shocks suggests that market participants in these ASEAN countries react more strongly to negative information, which could be due to various factors, including investor sentiment or market structure. For Indonesia, the external regressors (λ1 and λ2) are statistically insignificant, indicating that the election did not generate abnormal volatility either before or after the event. This may be due to a relatively stable political environment or predictable election outcomes. The predictability of election outcomes can be linked to the influence of pre-electoral coalitions (PECs. Candidates backed by strong PECs are significantly more likely to win elections, particularly non-incumbents (Lewis, 2020). In contrast, Malaysia shows a significant pre-election effect (λ1) but an insignificant post-election effect (λ2). That indicates uncertainty before the election had a more pronounced impact on volatility than the election results themselves (Jiun, 2018). Thailand and the Philippines exhibit significant values for both λ1 and λ2, implying elevated volatility during both the pre- and post-election periods. In Thailand, this may be attributed to political party manipulation and post-election instability, while in the Philippines, deep political divisions and uncertainty surrounding candidates likely contributed to continued volatility. These findings indicate that in some Southeast Asian markets, elections create sustained volatility due to ongoing political uncertainty, while in others, the market response is concentrated in the pre-election period. The high significance levels suggest that these markets are sensitive to broader economic conditions or external shocks captured by these variables (Panjaitan & Saadah, 2018). Several macroeconomic factors contributed to significant changes in the stock markets during the presidential election periods. In Indonesia, political riots, social media sarcasm, and demonstrations exacerbated market volatility (Wong & Hooy, 2016). In Malaysia, political manipulation led to investor unease, resulting in lower stock prices due to concerns about long- term market impacts (Wong & Hooy, 2016). Thailand, known for political party manipulations, witnessed deliberate efforts by top officials to influence elections (Jiajanpong et al., 2022). Similarly, in the Philippines, political divisions over presidential candidates led to increased political tension and market volatility (Macrohon et al., 2022). While the results offer valuable insights into how elections affect stock volatility in Southeast Asia, it is important to consider market microstructure noise—such as variations in trading volume, liquidity, and bid-ask spreads—that could distort stock price movements during election periods at high frequencies (Awartani et al., 2009) and may lead to an increased observed price variance (Couleau et al., 2019). Election periods are often associated with heightened market volatility due to uncertainty surrounding election outcomes. This volatility is influenced by the accuracy of pre-election polls and discrepancies between expected and actual results (Nguyen et al., 2023). Historical data shows that stock exchanges tend to rise before elections and fall afterwards, indicating price anomalies during electoral periods (Nguyen, 2022). However, market https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Akbar et al. (2026) 8 microstructure issues may obscure the true relationship between political events and volatility, as factors beyond political uncertainty can influence investor behaviour. Additionally, country-specific political dynamics may influence the generalizability of the findings. Although this study examines countries with similar political systems, variations in each country’s electoral process, political stability, and institutional quality can lead to differing policy outcomes, which in turn may affect market reactions and limit the broader applicability of the results (Rontos et al., 2015; Younsi & Bechtini, 2019). For example, Indonesia has experienced post-election disputes and a lack of transparency in some elections, which could influence stock market behaviour (Kusdarini et al., 2022). In Malaysia, political patronage and clientelism may affect investor confidence, contributing to volatility (Aspinall & Hicken, 2020). Similarly, political challenges in Thailand and the Philippines, including military influences and deep divisions among voters, could create distinct volatility patterns influenced not just by elections but by the broader political context (Chambers, 2024). While this study relies on LogL for model selection as a good fit for the data (Jones, 2011), incorporating the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) alongside LogL would provide a more comprehensive evaluation of the model selection process. AIC and BIC are valuable tools for assessing the trade-off between model fit and complexity, with AIC focusing on minimising the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the true model and the approximating model (Darnius et al., 2019; Ghahramani, 2014; Seghouane & Amari, 2007). On the other hand, BIC imposes a stronger penalty for model complexity, offering a more stringent approach to model selection (Burnham & Anderson, 2004; Neath & Cavanaugh, 2012). Using AIC, BIC, and LogL together allows for a more balanced evaluation of model fit and complexity. 4. Conclusions and recommendations This paper examined the impact of presidential elections on stock return volatility in four Southeast Asian countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines. The study revealed that political uncertainty before elections significantly heightened stock market volatility across all four nations. Additionally, the analysis demonstrated that the uncertainty surrounding post-election policies and investor understanding of these policies further amplified market volatility for up to 90 days after the election. The results confirm that elections indeed influence market behaviour, with significant declines in stock prices observed post-election, underscoring the role of political events in shaping market dynamics. The findings suggest that these countries are perceived as risky by investors during election periods, driven by unrest, demonstrations, and political tensions. This volatility can lead to capital flight, as investors seek safer investment opportunities. Such movements can also cause currency depreciation, which may destabilise the macroeconomic environment. Policymakers should consider these risks and review the political and institutional frameworks governing elections to reduce uncertainty and bolster investor confidence. We also recommend that investors be aware of the political environment and its potential impacts on stock market volatility. Understanding how political events, such as elections, can affect market dynamics is crucial for making informed investment decisions. Conducting sector-specific analyses during election periods could provide deeper insights into which sectors are most vulnerable or resilient to political uncertainties. This approach would help investors better navigate election- induced market fluctuations and make more strategic choices. Since this study focused on the selected market, future research could explore how different sectors respond to election-related volatility. For example, sectors such as energy and consumer goods may exhibit varying levels of volatility depending on political events. Analysing these sectors individually could offer a more nuanced understanding of how specific elections impact industries. Additionally, future studies could expand the scope to include a comparative regional analysis. This would involve examining the effects of elections in both developing and developed countries, offering a broader perspective on how political uncertainty influences stock markets across different economic contexts. Comparing regions with differing political and economic structures could reveal valuable insights into how political events affect market reactions in diverse settings. JSON: Name: pres_election_volatility_sub_asean Title: Comparative GJR-GARCH analysis of the impact of presidential elections on stock return volatility in Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines Short Hypothesis: Presidential election periods (defined as the 90 trading days before and after the official election date) cause a statistically significant increase in conditional stock return volatility in Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines as evidenced by positive and significant pre-election and/or post-election dummy coefficients in GJR-GARCH(1,1) estimates relative to non-election periods. Related Work: Prior work on political-event effects in equity markets has relied primarily on heteroskedastic time-series models (GARCH family), event-study frameworks, and realized-volatility measures. Comparative studies are sparse: most analyses focus on single countries or single elections and therefore do not assess cross-country commonalities. Existing volatility-modeling approaches include symmetric GARCH(1,1) which captures clustering but misses asymmetry, EGARCH which models log-variance and leverage, and GJR-GARCH which introduces indicator-based asymmetry; model selection has often relied on single criteria or visual fit. Shortcomings in prior work include limited use of asymmetric models in comparative settings, inconsistent pre-whitening or thin-trading adjustments, insufficient robustness checks (alternative window lengths, distributional assumptions, or information criteria), sparse out-of-sample forecast evaluation, and limited consideration of market microstructure noise and country heterogeneity. These gaps limit confidence in generalizing the political-uncertainty–volatility relationship across similar emerging markets. Abstract: This research quantifies the effect of presidential elections on stock return volatility in four sub-ASEAN markets: Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, and the Philippines. We propose a comparative time-series pipeline that (1) pre-whitens daily index returns with AR(1) filtering, (2) selects among symmetric and asymmetric GARCH-type specifications using log-likelihood, AIC and BIC, and (3) estimates GJR-GARCH(1,1) models extended with 90-day pre-election and 90-day post-election dummy regressors in the conditional variance. The main contribution is a cross-country assessment of election-induced volatility that explicitly models leverage effects and contrasts model choices and forecast performance across markets. Expected outcomes are statistically quantified pre- and post-election impacts on conditional variance, model selection guidance for election-event volatility studies in emerging markets, and empirical evidence on persistence and asymmetry of election-driven shocks. Results will inform investors and researchers about the timing and magnitude of election-related volatility across comparable Southeast Asian equity markets. Experiments: Datasets: - Daily closing prices of benchmark equity indices: Indonesia (IDX Composite), Malaysia (FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI), Thailand (SET Index), Philippines (PSEi). - Sample period: 01-Jan-2014 to 31-Dec-2024 (or available coverage), with focus windows of ±90 trading days around each presidential election date listed in the report. - Derived series: continuously compounded daily returns, squared returns, and realized volatility proxies (daily squared returns). If available, include 5-minute intraday returns for realized-variance robustness checks. Baselines: 1) GARCH(1,1) without election dummies. 2) EGARCH(1,1) with election dummies. 3) GJR-GARCH(1,1) without election dummies. Proposed primary model: GJR-GARCH(1,1) with two variance regressors: preelect (1 for 90 trading days before election, else 0) and postelect (1 for 90 trading days after election, else 0). Model selection and estimation: - Fit each model per country using maximum likelihood under two error distributions: Gaussian and Student-t. - Use LogL, AIC, BIC to select preferred model per country. Evaluation metrics: - In-sample: Log-Likelihood, AIC, BIC, statistical significance (t-stats) of preelect and postelect coefficients (λ1, λ2), parameter stability. - Residual diagnostics: Ljung-Box Q on standardized residuals and squared residuals, ARCH-LM p-values. - Forecasting: one-step-ahead variance forecasts evaluated out-of-sample using rolling windows (estimation window=1500 trading days, 1-step rolling forecast), compute RMSE and MAE of predicted variance vs realized variance proxy; use Diebold-Mariano tests for forecast comparisons. Comparisons / Ablations: - Compare GJR-GARCH vs EGARCH vs GARCH on model selection and forecast metrics. - Ablation A: drop preelect dummy to test isolated post-election effect. - Ablation B: drop postelect dummy to test isolated pre-election effect. - Ablation C: remove leverage term (Γ) to assess asymmetry contribution. - Sensitivity tests: vary election window lengths (±30, ±60, ±180 trading days) and error distributions (Gaussian vs t) and report λ1/λ2 sign, magnitude, and significance. - Cross-country pooled test: estimate panel-GARCH specification pooling indices with country fixed effects versus separate country models and compare coefficient homogeneity via likelihood ratio tests. Implementation details: - Preprocessing: AR(1) pre-whitening, winsorize extreme returns at 0.1% tails, align election day to next trading day when necessary. - Significance threshold: two-sided 5%. - Report: parameter estimates, SEs, diagnostic tests, out-of-sample forecast tables and Diebold-Mariano p-values. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: misspecification of conditional variance form (GJR-GARCH may not capture all dynamics), nonstationarity or structural breaks in return-generating process, incorrect error distribution leading to biased inference. Data limitations: limited number of election events per country reduces statistical power; uneven sample lengths across countries; potential missing or unreliable intraday data for realized-volatility robustness checks. Evaluation biases: use of daily squared returns as realized-variance proxy is noisy and sensitive to microstructure effects; event-window choice (±90 days) may confound other macroeconomic shocks. Scalability / compute: maximum-likelihood estimation with heavy-tailed distributions and rolling forecasts across multiple models and countries increases compute time but is tractable on standard servers. Generalization limits: results apply to the four selected sub-ASEAN markets and the sampled elections; findings may not generalize to other countries, parliamentary elections, or non-presidential political events. Causal attribution limits: GARCH-based associations cannot fully isolate causal mechanisms from concurrent macroeconomic or global shocks.
